title: Statistical Machine Learning & Data Analytics
text:
How to use this booklet
This is the exercise booklet for Module 3 of the Health Data Science MSc. It is organised by teaching day: each day is a part of the book, and each chapter inside a day is one exercise you can finish in a single sitting.
Each exercise is code to read and copy. The worked examples are shown with the output they produce, so you can compare your own result against ours. You run the code in R or Python on your own machine or vlab.
Tasks appear as code containing ______ for you to fill in. They are shown but not run, which is why no output appears beneath them.

title: Statistical Machine Learning & Data Analytics
text:
Why both languages
Most health data science teams use one language for data management and the other for modelling, and the ability to read a colleague’s code in the language you do not prefer is worth more than fluency in either. Every exercise therefore has an R path and a Python path doing the same work, in tabs. Pay attention to where both differ.

title: 1  Exercise 1.1 — Python vs R
text:
1.1 The libraries
A note on vocabulary. R calls them packages and loads them with library(dplyr); Python calls them modules or packages and loads them with import pandas as pd or from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score. Then in R, library(dplyr) puts every dplyr function within reach, whereas Python makes you name what you want. That is why R code reads filter(...) and Python code reads pd.read_csv(...) — the prefix tells you where the function came from, and in R you have to remember.






TipExtra






Try out dplyr::filter() in R does it work?





Key R packages

The tidyverse — getting data into shape
tidyverse is not one package but a family that shares a design: data frames in, data frames out, verbs that read as English (for example, a dplyr pipeline is a sentence. data |> filter(age > 60) |> summarise(mean(los)) reads left to right in the order the work happens) and the pipe (|> or %>%) to chain them. library(tidyverse) loads them all at once. The key packages tidyversecontains are:



Package
What it does




readr
reads .csv into a data frame — read_csv()


dplyr
the verbs: filter, select, mutate, group_by, summarise, arrange


ggplot2
plots built by adding layers — ggplot() + geom_point()


tidyr
reshaping between wide and long — pivot_longer()






tidymodels — fitting and evaluating
tidymodels is also a collection of packages.It is to modelling what the tidyverse is to data handling: a family of packages with one grammar. Its central idea is that specifying a model is separate from fitting it, and separate again from which implementation does the arithmetic. Key packages it contains are:



Package
What it does




parsnip
one vocabulary for many models — linear_reg(), logistic_reg(), rand_forest()


recipes
preprocessing as a fitted object — step_normalize(), step_impute_mean()


rsample
splitting and resampling — initial_split(), vfold_cv()


yardstick
evaluation metrics — rmse(), roc_auc(), sens(), spec()



To call a specific ML algorithm you set an engine. For example, set_engine("ranger") means “fit this random forest using the ranger package”. The specification stays the same; the engine is swapped.



Engine
Package
Used for




"lm", "glm"
base R
linear and logistic regression


"rpart"
rpart
a single decision tree


"ranger"
ranger
random forests, fast


"glmnet"
glmnet
lasso and ridge





Key Python packages


The scientific stack



Library
What it does




pandas
the DataFrame — read_csv(), groupby(), describe()


numpy
arrays and the maths on them; what pandas is built on


matplotlib
plots, built by commanding an Axes object


scipy
scientific algorithms; here optimize.minimize





scikit-learn
In scikit-learn every object follows the same contract: .fit(X, y) learns from data, .transform(X) or .predict(X) applies what was learned, and .fit_transform() does both. Once you know that, a model you have never seen before is usable in one line.
It is organised into submodules and here are a few to note:







Submodule
What lives there




linear_model
LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Lasso


model_selection
train_test_split, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV


metrics
mean_absolute_error, roc_auc_score, confusion_matrix


preprocessing
StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, OneHotEncoder


pipeline
Pipeline — the object that makes leakage hard to commit


compose
ColumnTransformer — different preprocessing per column


impute
SimpleImputer, IterativeImputer


tree, ensemble
DecisionTreeClassifier, RandomForestClassifier


inspection
permutation_importance, partial_dependence


dummy
DummyClassifier — the baseline you must beat



The scikit-learn user guide explains the statistics as well as the code, and is worth reading.

What differs is what each returns. lm() hands back a statistical summary — standard errors, residuals, an F test — because R’s linear model was written for inference. LinearRegression hands back coefficients and a .predict() method, because scikit-learn’s was written for prediction.
R can also do it the scikit-learn/ML way. tidymodels sets the model up in the same three moves — define the algorithm, give it the data, fit it:

library(tidymodels)

lm_model <- linear_reg() %>%
            set_engine("lm") %>%      # use lm()'s implementation underneath

1.8 Algebra:numpy → base R
numpy is Python’s array library; in R, arrays and the arithmetic on them are in the language itself (preloaded package called base) , so there is nothing to load. Here, a dot product.

RPython



a <- c(1, 2, 3)
b <- c(4, 5, 6)
dot_product <- sum(a * b)
dot_product

#> [1] 32





import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
dot_product = np.dot(a, b)
print(dot_product)

#> 32





a * b multiplies element by element in both languages, and sum() adds the result. np.dot does both in one step. Check out %*% too

title: 2  Exercise 1.2 — Your first ML pipeline
text:
2.1 Overview
In this exercise you will build your first machine learning pipeline, using a linear regression algorithm. A pipeline is a sequence of reproducible steps that takes raw data and produces predictions.
The structure matters because we want models that work beyond the rows we fitted them to. You have already built a linear regression in the previous Module 2 (statistics). Here the same model sits inside a workflow with extra steps, whose job is to test how well it performs on new, unseen data. That workflow keeps growing over the next few days as we add concepts to it.
The five steps
Step 3 is what separates this from Module 2. In statistics you fit to all the data and ask whether a relationship is real. In machine learning you hold rows back and ask whether the model is any use on rows it has never seen.

NoteToday’s validation is the simplest possible one



We use a train/test split: the model learns from one subset and is scored on another. It is easy to follow and it makes generalisation concrete, which is why we start here.
BUT
It is also wasteful and unstable. A single split uses the data inefficiently, and the score depends on which rows happened to land in the test set. In the following days you will learn about the concept of resampling: cross-validation, repeated splits and bootstrapping, which let us evaluate more reliably, tune more effectively, and get more out of a limited dataset.

2) Say what predicts what
This is the first place the two languages genuinely differ. scikit-learn wants the predictors and the outcome handed over as separate objects. tidymodels takes them as a formula at the moment of fitting, so there is nothing to do here — which is why the right-hand column is empty until step 4.

# 1-D: the outcome

R
Nothing to define yet. The formula LOS ~ Age + Severity in step 4 says the same thing, at the point where it is used.


The double brackets are not a typo. scikit-learn wants a matrix of predictors and a vector of outcomes, and df["Age"] would give it a vector where it expects a matrix.

#> (np.float64(-8.35120447047774), array([0.92877698, 3.4711372 ]))





R

los_model <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm")

los_fit <- los_model %>%
  fit(LOS ~ Age + Severity, data = train)

        file.path(tempdir(),
                  "los_fit_model.RDS"))



In your own project you would save it beside your script — joblib.dump(model, "los_fit_model.pkl") or saveRDS(los_fit, "los_fit_model.RDS"). Here it goes to a temporary folder so the booklet does not leave files behind.
On the R side, notice that linear_reg() fits nothing and mentions no data. The specification says linear regression, computed by lm and stops there. That separation is what lets you swap the algorithm later without touching the rest — and it is the step scikit-learn folds into the one LinearRegression() call above.


5) Evaluate on the test set
To say whether the predictions are any good we have to measure them. We use the mean absolute error: take the absolute difference between each prediction and the truth, then average over the test set.
\[
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left| y_i - \hat{y}_i \right|
\]
Because we are predicting length of stay, MAE tells us how many days our predictions are wrong by, on average.


Python

pred_test = model.predict(X_test)
mae_test = mean_absolute_error(y_test,
                               pred_test)
mae_test

#> 3.158914339767372





R

test_pred <- predict(los_fit, test) %>%
  bind_cols(test)

mae(test_pred, truth = LOS,
    estimate = .pred)

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 mae     standard        3.42




Later in the module we will check other available metrics such as RMSE, R² and median absolute error, and look at when each is preferable.


6) Visualise predicted against actual


Python

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(y_test, pred_test, alpha=0.5)
lo = min(y_test.min(), pred_test.min())
hi = max(y_test.max(), pred_test.max())
# the 45 degree line: perfect prediction
ax.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi])
ax.set_xlabel("Actual LOS (days)")
ax.set_ylabel("Predicted LOS (days)")
plt.show()











R

ggplot(test_pred, aes(x = LOS, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Actual LOS (days)",
       y = "Predicted LOS (days)") +
  coord_equal()










A perfect model would put every point on the diagonal. How far the cloud sits from that line, and whether it drifts away from it at one end, is the whole story of the model in one picture.







WarningWhy the two MAEs are not the same number



set.seed(42) and random_state=42 do not select the same rows. They are different generators, and the seed is not a shared address. So the two languages have different test sets and different scores — ours differ by about 0.3 days.
That is expected. What would be a problem is a difference large enough to change your conclusion. Both numbers are near 3.2 to 3.4 days, so both support the same statement. Cross-validation later replaces the single split, after which the two agree much more closely, because the score stops depending on one arbitrary partition.

3.1 Summary Statistics
Histograms show the overall shape and spread of the data distribution and box plots summarise key statistics (median, spread, and potential outliers) and are particularly helpful for comparing distributions across groups.
#Remember, if you do not have these packages installed, install them first with (install.packages()). In These packages will allow us to access the functions we need to perform our analysis. 

library(ggplot2) #plotting - part of tidyverse
library(patchwork) #have side by side plots 
library(gapminder) #gives us acess to a dataset
library(tidyverse) #gives us access to all other libraries available in tidyverse. In reality would not need ggplot loaded as separate library if have already tidyverse loaded!
# Example data
data <- data.frame(age = c(2,  45, 56, 47, 67, 67, 68, 72, 75, 80, 85,86, 89,125))
head(data)

#>   age
#> 1   2
#> 2  45
#> 3  56
#> 4  47
#> 5  67
#> 6  67
What is the distribution of the age data? What are the mean, median and standard deviation?
Mean <- mean(data$age)
Median <- median(data$age)
Sd <- sd(data$age)
Other data distribution descriptors include quantiles, which divide data into equal-sized intervals:
0% (Minimum) 25% (Q1, First Quartile) 50% (Median, Second Quartile) 75% (Q3, Third Quartile) *100% (Maximum)
Quantile <- quantile(data$age)
Quantile

#>     0%    25%    50%    75%   100% 
#>   2.00  58.75  70.00  83.75 125.00
The IQR (Interquartile Range) measures the spread of the middle 50% of your data.
If you look at the Quantile results above, you can calculate it from \(IQR=Q3−Q1\), where Q3 is the value beyond which 75% of your data lies. What is then Q2? The value beyond which 25% of your data lies.
IQR <- IQR(data$age)
IQR

#> [1] 25
Can do it in a single go:
summary(data$age) 

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    2.00   58.75   70.00   68.86   83.75  125.00
As we saw, lots of different datasets can end up with these summary statistics, so lets plot it to get real insight about what is happening:

3.2 Histogram in R
A histogram is a way to visualise the frequency distribution of a dataset. It groups data into bins and shows how many data points fall into each bin

  geom_histogram() 








You can modify the binwidth parameter, what is happening here?

Now lets go back t original and add the mean and median

  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Mean, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Median, color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1)








If do not remember how ggplot works , here is a cheatsheet: https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html
In summary, a histogram helps you understand the shape of your data distribution (e.g., normal, skewed) and peaks indicate the most frequent values.

title: 3  Exercise 2.1 — Histograms and boxplots
text:
3.3 Box Plot in R
A box plot (or box-and-whisker plot) summarises the distribution of a dataset. It highlights:

Median (middle line in the box).
Quantiles (the box spans from the 25th percentile to the 75th percentile)
IQR (Interquartile Range): The difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles - (IQR range calculated above)
Whiskers: Extend to data points within 1.5*IQR (above or beyond = outliers)


ggplot(data, aes(x = age)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  coord_flip() #have you checked what this does? Take it out and see








Can you see summary statistics mapped here?
Lets plot the mean (as it is a value that is not reflected in a boxplot!)

ggplot(data, aes(x = age)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  coord_flip() + 
   geom_vline(xintercept = Mean, color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) 








For an extra challenge, add another geom layer, i.e geom_jitter. What does it do? How is it different from geom_point?
Now, lets go a step further. If we want to understand how the data varies by groups, we can use facets:

ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = "age" )) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  geom_jitter() +
  coord_flip() + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = Mean, color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) 









# Sample data
set.seed(123)

data <- data.frame(
  Group = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 200),
  Value = c(rnorm(200, mean = 5, sd = 1), 
            rnorm(200, mean = 6, sd = 1.2), 
            rnorm(200, mean = 7, sd = 1.5))
)


# Combined Plot
p1 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Group, y = Value, fill = Group)) +
  # Violin + Boxplot + Jitter
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.color = "red", outlier.size = 2, colour = "black") +
  geom_jitter(position = position_jitter(0.2), color = "black", alpha = 0.4) + #scatter plot but in random positions, check geom_point() and see
  labs(title = "Boxplot and Violin Plot with Jitter", x = "Groups", y = "Values") +
  theme_minimal()


p2 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Value, fill = Group)) +
  # Histogram
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", binwidth = 0.3, colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Values by Group", x = "Values", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()


# Display both plots side by side (thanks to having patchwork installed)

p1 + p2









# Display both plots up down

p1 / p2








Lets use this in another dataset (gapminder dataset that we have access to, thanks to the loaded package gapminder)

# Box plot with facets by year
ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = continent, y = lifeExp, fill = continent)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +  # Create facets for each year
  labs(title = "Life Expectancy Across Continents by Year",
       x = "Continent",
       y = "Life Expectancy") +
  theme_minimal() + #just to make it nice
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))  # Rotate x-axis labels - just to make it nice

  filter(year == "1952") %>%
  filter(continent == "Africa")

Median

4.1 Correlation
This is an example of the great amount of resources available in open-source programming languages, where new packages are developed and made available constantly. As key insight, explore, probably what you need is already out there for you to use!
For you to see the breadth of possibilities out there, here is an example of different ways in which to describe and learn about the correlation matrix of your dataset.
# Install required libraries (if not already installed)

#install.packages(c("ggplot2", "corrplot", "ggcorrplot", 
#"PerformanceAnalytics", "GGally", "psych", "corrr"))

# Load necessary libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(corrplot)
library(ggcorrplot)
library(PerformanceAnalytics)
library(GGally)
library(psych)
library(corrr)
To assess the association between two variables, you can produce a scatter plot like below:
set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- x + rnorm(100, sd = 0.5)

ggplot(data = data.frame(x, y), aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Correlation Plot with ggplot2",
       x = "X values", y = "Y values") +
  theme_minimal()
Now we are going to produce the correlation matrix, where in a go, you get insight of all the association happening in your dataset.For this we are going to use the mtcars data (A built-in dataset that contains measurements on 11 different attributes for 32 different cars). More specifically, the chosen variables are:
data <- mtcars[, c("mpg", "disp", "hp", "wt")]
Can you calculate the correlation between them? Try out at least a pair of functions/packages. Remember there are different ways in which to calculate correlation https://www.sthda.com/english/wiki/correlation-test-between-two-variables-in-r and you can specify the type in your code cor(x, y, method = c("pearson", "kendall", "spearman"))
Now that you know what to expect, lets proceed with the correlation matrices (same thing as above, but all in a go!):

4.2 What a correlation does with values that are not real
mtcars is clean. Clinical files are not, and the usual way they are not clean is that somebody recorded an absent measurement as a number. Before trusting any of the matrices above, look at data/diabetes.csv: 768 adults, eight measurements and an outcome.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")

diabetes |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ sum(.x == 0))) |>
  t()

#>          [,1]
#> pregnant   80
#> glucose     5
#> pressure   35
#> triceps   251
#> insulin   405
#> mass       13
#> pedigree    0
#> age         0


A plasma glucose of zero is not a low reading, and a body mass index of zero is not a thin patient. Both are impossible, so the zero is standing in for “not measured”. Replace the impossible ones with NA and compare the two matrices:

cols <- c("glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass")

dia_na <- diabetes |>
  mutate(across(all_of(cols), ~ na_if(.x, 0)))

round(cor(diabetes[cols]), 2)

#>          glucose pressure triceps insulin mass
#> glucose     1.00     0.05    0.03    0.31 0.18
#> pressure    0.05     1.00    0.21    0.16 0.38
#> triceps     0.03     0.21    1.00    0.47 0.38
#> insulin     0.31     0.16    0.47    1.00 0.22
#> mass        0.18     0.38    0.38    0.22 1.00

round(cor(dia_na[cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 2)

#>          glucose pressure triceps insulin mass
#> glucose     1.00     0.09    0.16    0.52 0.19
#> pressure    0.09     1.00    0.11    0.13 0.24
#> triceps     0.16     0.11    1.00    0.17 0.61
#> insulin     0.52     0.13    0.17    1.00 0.20
#> mass        0.19     0.24    0.61    0.20 1.00








WarningThe result that should bother you



The strongest association in the raw matrix is mostly an artefact of the zeros, and one of the real associations was hidden by them. Both directions, in the same table.

insulin with triceps falls from about 0.47 to about 0.17 once the zeros are treated as missing. Every one of the 251 rows with a zero skin-fold also has a zero insulin, so a quarter of the file sits exactly at the origin of that scatter plot. Points at the origin, far below the real values, pull a regression line through themselves. The association was between the two recording failures, not between the two hormonal quantities.
triceps with mass rises from about 0.38 to about 0.61. Skin-fold thickness and body mass index measure overlapping things and should agree; the zeros were diluting that agreement towards the middle.
So the zeros did not add noise. Noise attenuates everything. They moved correlations, up for pairs that share a missingness pattern and down for pairs that do not — and nothing in the output marks which is which.

5.2 Why this, here
Chapter 4 left you with a complete table of numbers. Models are sensitive to the scale and the shape of those numbers in ways that have nothing to do with the clinical content: a variable measured in thousands dominates one measured in units, and a long right tail puts most of the leverage in a handful of patients. This exercise is about what the common fixes actually do — including the one that does nothing.

data/bupa.csv holds 345 patients with five liver-related blood tests (mcv, alkalinephosphotase, alamine, aspartate, gammaGlut), a count of daily alcoholic drinks, and a column called selector. There are no missing values.






Warningselector is not a diagnosis



It is the field the original depositors used to split the file into two sets, 200 rows and 145 rows. Tutorials across the internet model it as a liver disease label; it is not one, and a model that predicts it is predicting an arbitrary partition. Compare the mean and the median of gammaGlut, then of mcv. In one of them they agree; in the other the mean is half as large again as the median. That gap is the fingerprint of a right tail, and skewness puts a number on it.
\[g_1 = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^3}{\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2\right]^{3/2}}\]
Zero for a symmetric variable, positive when the tail is to the right. Above about 1 it is worth doing something about; above 2 the mean is no longer a useful summary. section: 5.5 The result that should bother you
text:
5.5 The result that should bother you
Min-max scaling and standardisation leave the skewness exactly where it was. Only the log moves it, from about 2.9 to about 0.5.

Both scalings are affine: they multiply by one constant and subtract another. Skewness is built from the ratio of the third and second central moments, and that ratio is unchanged by multiplication — the constant cancels, top and bottom. The number is identical, not approximately identical.
So “normalising” the data does not make it normal. It makes it comparable, which is a different problem, solved for a different reason: a distance, a penalty or a gradient step treats a variable in thousands differently from one in units.
The log is the only one of the three that changes the shape, because it is not affine. It also changes the meaning: a coefficient fitted to log(gammaGlut) is about proportional change, not absolute, and that is something you have to be willing to say in the discussion section.

See it rather than take it on trust: three boxplots of the same variable.

5.7 Task 2 — Where the log is not available
drinks is right-skewed too, and nine patients report zero. log(0) is -Inf, which propagates into every summary and plot downstream.
Try log(drinks) first and look at what you get. Then use log1p(), which computes \(\log(1 + x)\), and compare the skewness of both against the raw column.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.

title: 6  Exercise 2.4 — Leakage
text:
6.2 Why this, here
Everything you did today was fitted to the whole file. The median that filled the gaps in Chapter 4 was computed from all 200 patients; the mean and standard deviation in Chapter 5 came from all 345. On Day 1 you learned to hold rows back so that the evaluation means something (Chapter 2). Those two habits are in direct conflict, and this exercise is about which one wins.
The rule is short: anything learned from data is part of the model, and must be learned from the training rows only. A log is not learned. A mean is. So is a median, a standard deviation, a minimum, a set of category levels, an imputation model, and the choice of which predictors to keep.

title: 6  Exercise 2.4 — Leakage
text:
6.4 Leak 1 — Scaling before the split
The textbook mistake. Standardise the predictors using the mean and standard deviation of all 755 rows, then split, then fit. Compare with standardising using the training rows only. For both, fill the gaps the same way, so that the only difference is where the scaling constants came from.

RPython



preds <- c("triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant")
fill_na <- function(df, values) {
  for (v in names(values)) df[[v]][is.na(df[[v]])] <- values[[v]]
  df
}
train_means <- lapply(train[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
train_f <- fill_na(train, train_means)
test_f  <- fill_na(test,  train_means)

# WRONG: centre and scale using every row, training and test together
all_f  <- fill_na(dia, train_means)
mu_all <- sapply(all_f[preds], mean); sd_all <- sapply(all_f[preds], sd)
scale_by <- function(df, mu, sd) {
  for (v in names(mu)) df[[v]] <- (df[[v]] - mu[[v]]) / sd[[v]]
  df
}
model_formula <- mass ~ triceps + pressure + age + pregnant
fit_leak  <- lm(model_formula, data = scale_by(train_f, mu_all, sd_all))
mae_scale_leak <- mean(abs(test_f$mass -
  predict(fit_leak, scale_by(test_f, mu_all, sd_all))))

# RIGHT: constants from the training rows only
mu_tr <- sapply(train_f[preds], mean); sd_tr <- sapply(train_f[preds], sd)
fit_ok <- lm(model_formula, data = scale_by(train_f, mu_tr, sd_tr))
mae_scale_ok <- mean(abs(test_f$mass -
  predict(fit_ok, scale_by(test_f, mu_tr, sd_tr))))

c(leaky = mae_scale_leak, honest = mae_scale_ok,
  difference = mae_scale_leak - mae_scale_ok)

#>        leaky       honest   difference 
#> 4.457562e+00 4.457562e+00 8.881784e-16





from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

preds = ["triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant"]
imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit(train[preds])
train_f = pd.DataFrame(imp.transform(train[preds]), columns=preds, index=train.index)
test_f  = pd.DataFrame(imp.transform(test[preds]),  columns=preds, index=test.index)
all_f   = pd.DataFrame(imp.transform(dia[preds]),   columns=preds, index=dia.index)

# WRONG: scaler fitted on every row, training and test together
sc_leak = StandardScaler().fit(all_f)
fit_leak = LinearRegression().fit(sc_leak.transform(train_f), train["mass"])
mae_scale_leak = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_leak.predict(sc_leak.transform(test_f)))

# RIGHT: scaler fitted on the training rows only
sc_ok = StandardScaler().fit(train_f)
fit_ok = LinearRegression().fit(sc_ok.transform(train_f), train["mass"])
mae_scale_ok = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_ok.predict(sc_ok.transform(test_f)))

print(mae_scale_leak, mae_scale_ok, mae_scale_leak - mae_scale_ok)

#> 4.924484517271224 4.924484517271224 0.0





The two MAEs are the same number, and not approximately: they agree to the last decimal place the computer keeps, and the difference printed is floating-point arithmetic rather than statistics. This is not a near miss. It is an identity.
Standardisation subtracts a constant and divides by another. Ordinary least squares then estimates whatever coefficients undo that, exactly: scale a predictor by \(c\) and its coefficient becomes \(\beta/c\), so every fitted value is unchanged. The leak transferred information — the test rows did influence \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) — and the model had no way to use it.






WarningDo not conclude that scaling leakage is harmless



It is harmless here, because the model is linear and the leak is an affine transformation. Put a penalty on the coefficients, as ridge and lasso do, and the scale decides how hard each coefficient is pushed towards zero, so the leak changes the fit. Use a distance-based method and it changes the neighbours. The rule exists because you cannot audit, at the moment you write the preprocessing, every model that will later be fitted on top of it.

6.5 Task 1 — Leak 2: imputation before the split
Now the leak the original version of this material was most worried about. Fill the missing triceps and pressure with the mean of all 755 rows, then split and fit; then do it again with the mean of the training rows only. Report both MAEs and the difference.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
global_means <- lapply(dia[preds], mean, na.rm = ______)      # all rows: the leak
train_means  <- lapply(train[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE)

c(global_triceps = global_means$triceps, train_triceps = train_means$triceps)

fit_g <- lm(model_formula, data = fill_na(train, ______))
mae_imp_leak <- mean(abs(test$mass - predict(fit_g, fill_na(test, global_means))))

mae_imp_ok <- mean(abs(test$mass - predict(fit_t, fill_na(test, train_means))))

c(leaky = mae_imp_leak, honest = mae_imp_ok, difference = mae_imp_leak - mae_imp_ok)
c(model = mae_imp_ok, baseline = mae_baseline,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * mae_imp_ok / mae_baseline)







TipStuck?





fill_na() is defined above and takes a data frame and a named list of replacement values. The leaky version differs from the honest one by one argument: which frame the means were computed from.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
imp_leak = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit(______[preds])   # all rows: the leak
imp_ok   = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit(train[preds])

print(imp_leak.statistics_[0], imp_ok.statistics_[0])          # imputed triceps

fit_g = LinearRegression().fit(imp_leak.transform(train[preds]), train["mass"])
mae_imp_leak = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_g.predict(imp_leak.transform(test[preds])))

fit_t = LinearRegression().fit(imp_ok.transform(train[preds]), train["mass"])
mae_imp_ok = mean_absolute_error(
    test["mass"], fit_t.predict(imp_ok.transform(test[preds])))

print(mae_imp_leak, mae_imp_ok, mae_imp_leak - mae_imp_ok)
print(mae_imp_ok, mae_baseline, 100 * mae_imp_ok / mae_baseline)




This time the two numbers genuinely differ, because the imputed constant is data the model consumes rather than a rescaling it can absorb. They differ around the fourth decimal place of a quantity measured in BMI units, and which of them is larger depends on the split. The leak is real and it is worth nothing: a mean over 604 rows and a mean over 755 rows of the same population are nearly the same number, and the choice between them is not detectable in any result you would report.

title: 6  Exercise 2.4 — Leakage
section: 6.6 The result that should bother you
text:
6.6 The result that should bother you
Two leaks, carefully constructed, and the scoreboard is unchanged. If you stop here you will leave believing that the rule is a formality.
So try a third, and keep everything else the same. Impute the missing triceps and pressure by predicting them — a sensible thing to do, far better statistics than the mean — using a regression fitted to all 755 rows with every other column available to it, including mass, the outcome.

RPython



# WRONG: an imputation model fitted on all rows, allowed to see the outcome
dia_leak <- dia
for (v in c("triceps", "pressure")) {
  others <- c("mass", "age", "pregnant", "glucose")      # note what is in here
  usable <- complete.cases(dia_leak[others])
  m    <- lm(reformulate(others, v), data = dia_leak[usable & !is.na(dia_leak[[v]]), ])
  miss <- usable & is.na(dia_leak[[v]])
  dia_leak[[v]][miss] <- predict(m, newdata = dia_leak[miss, ])
}
dia_leak <- fill_na(dia_leak, lapply(dia_leak[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE))

train_leak <- dia_leak |> filter(row_id %in% train$row_id)
test_leak  <- dia_leak |> filter(row_id %in% test$row_id)

fit_leak3 <- lm(model_formula, data = train_leak)
mae_impmodel_leak <- mean(abs(test_leak$mass - predict(fit_leak3, test_leak)))

# RIGHT: the same idea, fitted on the training rows, outcome withheld
train_ok <- train; test_ok <- test
for (v in c("triceps", "pressure")) {
  others <- c("age", "pregnant", "glucose")              # and what is not
  m <- lm(reformulate(others, v),
          data = train_ok[complete.cases(train_ok[others]) & !is.na(train_ok[[v]]), ])
  for (nm in c("train_ok", "test_ok")) {
    d <- get(nm); miss <- complete.cases(d[others]) & is.na(d[[v]])
    d[[v]][miss] <- predict(m, newdata = d[miss, ]); assign(nm, d)
  }
}
train_ok <- fill_na(train_ok, lapply(train_ok[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE))
test_ok  <- fill_na(test_ok,  lapply(train_ok[preds], mean, na.rm = TRUE))

fit_ok3 <- lm(model_formula, data = train_ok)
mae_impmodel_ok <- mean(abs(test_ok$mass - predict(fit_ok3, test_ok)))

c(leaky = mae_impmodel_leak, honest = mae_impmodel_ok,
  difference = mae_impmodel_leak - mae_impmodel_ok)

#>      leaky     honest difference 
#>  3.7103182  4.4562384 -0.7459202





# WRONG: an imputation model fitted on all rows, allowed to see the outcome
dia_leak = dia.copy()
for v in ["triceps", "pressure"]:
    others = ["mass", "age", "pregnant", "glucose"]
    obs = dia_leak[v].notna() & dia_leak[others].notna().all(axis=1)
    m = LinearRegression().fit(dia_leak.loc[obs, others], dia_leak.loc[obs, v])
    miss = dia_leak[v].isna() & dia_leak[others].notna().all(axis=1)
    dia_leak.loc[miss, v] = m.predict(dia_leak.loc[miss, others])
dia_leak[preds] = dia_leak[preds].fillna(dia_leak[preds].mean())

train_leak, test_leak = dia_leak.loc[train.index], dia_leak.loc[test.index]
fit_leak3 = LinearRegression().fit(train_leak[preds], train_leak["mass"])
mae_impmodel_leak = mean_absolute_error(
    test_leak["mass"], fit_leak3.predict(test_leak[preds]))

# RIGHT: the same idea, fitted on the training rows, outcome withheld
train_ok, test_ok = train.copy(), test.copy()
for v in ["triceps", "pressure"]:
    others = ["age", "pregnant", "glucose"]
    obs = train_ok[v].notna() & train_ok[others].notna().all(axis=1)
    m = LinearRegression().fit(train_ok.loc[obs, others], train_ok.loc[obs, v])
    for d in (train_ok, test_ok):
        miss = d[v].isna() & d[others].notna().all(axis=1)
        d.loc[miss, v] = m.predict(d.loc[miss, others])
train_ok[preds] = train_ok[preds].fillna(train_ok[preds].mean())
test_ok[preds]  = test_ok[preds].fillna(train_ok[preds].mean())

fit_ok3 = LinearRegression().fit(train_ok[preds], train_ok["mass"])
mae_impmodel_ok = mean_absolute_error(
    test_ok["mass"], fit_ok3.predict(test_ok[preds]))

print(mae_impmodel_leak, mae_impmodel_ok, mae_impmodel_leak - mae_impmodel_ok)

#> 4.424760724778337 4.909747582230142 -0.4849868574518048





Now the number moves, by around half a BMI unit, and in the flattering direction. Over sixty different splits the leaky version won every single time, by between 0.3 and 0.8 units.

The imputation model learned triceps as a function of mass. Every imputed triceps in the test set is therefore a coded copy of that patient’s own BMI — the thing you are about to predict.
The outcome model then “discovers” that triceps predicts mass very well in exactly those rows, and the test MAE improves. Nothing was fabricated; the arithmetic is correct throughout. The test set simply stopped being held out.
This is why the rule is about information rather than about code order. Leak 1 moved a statistic across the split and cost nothing. Leak 3 moved the outcome across it, through a column that does not look like an outcome, and cost the entire evaluation.

The difference between leaks 2 and 3 is not how careless the analyst was. It is how much row-specific information the fitted step could carry. A mean carries almost none. A model carries as much as you let it.

section: 6.7 Task 2 — The leak-free pipeline, written once
text:
6.7 Task 2 — The leak-free pipeline, written once
Doing this by hand is how the mistakes get made, which is why both languages have a way to package preprocessing and model into one object that can only be fitted on what it is given.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rec <- recipe(mass ~ triceps + pressure + age + pregnant, data = ______) |>
  step_impute_mean(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"))

final <- last_fit(wf, split = split, metrics = metric_set(mae))
mae_pipeline <- collect_metrics(final)$.estimate
mae_pipeline
c(model = mae_pipeline, baseline = mae_baseline,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * mae_pipeline / mae_baseline)







TipStuck?





A recipe is declared against the frame whose structure it should learn from, and last_fit() then re-estimates every step on the training half of the split you hand it. Giving the recipe the test rows at this point would undo the thing you are demonstrating.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer

numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="mean")),
                    ("scale", StandardScaler())])
prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, preds)])
pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("model", LinearRegression())])

pipe.fit(______[preds], ______["mass"])
mae_pipeline = mean_absolute_error(test["mass"], pipe.predict(test[preds]))
print(mae_pipeline)
print(mae_pipeline, mae_baseline, 100 * mae_pipeline / mae_baseline)




The two objects are the same idea with different spelling. A recipe plus a workflow, or a ColumnTransformer inside a Pipeline: in both, fit() sees only the training rows, every fitted quantity is stored inside the object, and applying it to new data cannot consult that data. You get the leak-free behaviour because it is the only behaviour available, not because you remembered.

  step_normalize(all_predictors())
wf <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"))

mae_baseline <- mean(abs(test$mass - mean(train$mass)))
mae_once <- collect_metrics(last_fit(wf, split = split, metrics = metric_set(mae)))$.estimate
c(baseline = mae_baseline, one_split = mae_once)

#>  baseline one_split 
#>  5.556983  4.457562





import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
dia = diabetes.copy()
impossible = ["glucose", "pressure", "triceps", "insulin", "mass"]
dia[impossible] = dia[impossible].replace(0, np.nan)
dia = dia.dropna(subset=["mass"])[
    ["mass", "triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant", "glucose"]]
preds = ["triceps", "pressure", "age", "pregnant"]

def build_pipeline():
    numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="mean")),
                        ("scale", StandardScaler())])
    return Pipeline([("prep", ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, preds)])),
                     ("model", LinearRegression())])

train, test = train_test_split(dia, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

mae_baseline = np.abs(test["mass"] - train["mass"].mean()).mean()
pipe = build_pipeline().fit(train[preds], train["mass"])
mae_once = mean_absolute_error(test["mass"], pipe.predict(test[preds]))
print(mae_baseline, mae_once)

#> 5.865293188895224 4.924484517271224





One number each: 4.46 BMI units in R against a baseline of 5.56, and 4.92 against 5.87 in Python. These are the numbers Chapter 6 reported, and the question this exercise asks is what they are estimates of.
The pipeline is wrapped in a function in Python, and in a workflow in R, for a reason that matters below: both have to be refitted from scratch many times, and a fitted object carried over from one split to the next has already seen the rows the next split is about to hold out.

7.4 Task 1 — Fifty splits of the same data
Nothing about the data, the pipeline or the preprocessing changes. Only the random number that decides which 151 rows are held out. Repeat the whole pipeline 50 times, collect the 50 test MAEs, and report the lowest, the highest and the standard deviation.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.

one_split_mae <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(______)
  sp <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.8)
  collect_metrics(last_fit(wf, split = sp, metrics = metric_set(mae)))$.estimate
}

maes <- vapply(1:50, one_split_mae, numeric(1))
c(lowest = min(maes), highest = max(maes), spread = max(maes) - min(maes),
  mean = mean(maes), sd = ______)
sd(maes)   # expect 0.1 to 0.5







TipStuck?





vapply() applies a function to each element of a vector and returns a vector of a declared type; the function it is given here takes one seed and returns one MAE. last_fit() re-estimates every recipe step on the training half of whichever split it is handed, so the workflow built above can be reused unchanged. The spread of a sample is sd().






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.

def one_split_mae(seed):
    tr, te = train_test_split(dia, test_size=0.2, random_state=______)
    p = build_pipeline().fit(tr[preds], tr["mass"])
    return mean_absolute_error(te["mass"], p.predict(te[preds]))

maes = np.array([one_split_mae(s) for s in range(1, 51)])
print(f"lowest {maes.min():.3f} highest {maes.max():.3f} "
      f"spread {np.ptp(maes):.3f} mean {maes.mean():.3f} "
      f"sd {______:.3f}")
print(maes.std(ddof=1))   # expect 0.1 to 0.5







TipStuck?





build_pipeline() returns a new unfitted pipeline each time it is called, which is what the loop needs. For the spread, np.ndarray has a .std() method, and its ddof= argument decides whether you get the population or the sample standard deviation; the sample one is what you want here.






The fifty numbers run from 4.01 to 5.20 in R and from 4.13 to 5.26 in Python: a spread of about 1.1 to 1.2 BMI units, produced by nothing but the choice of seed. The standard deviation is 0.28 in R and 0.21 in Python.
Now put that next to the result of Chapter 6. The difference between the honest pipeline and the worst leak measured there was about half a BMI unit. The difference between two equally honest analysts who each ran this pipeline once, with different seeds, can be twice that. Every conclusion Day 2 drew by comparing pipelines on one split was drawn against a ruler with that much play in it.
Worse, you cannot tell from one run which draw you got. Seed 42 is in the fifty. In R its MAE is the nineteenth smallest of the fifty and sits 0.13 below their mean; in Python the same number 42 gives the forty-eighth of fifty, 0.38 above the mean and among the worst draws available. Two students, two languages, the same code: one of them would have reported a pipeline that looks slightly better than it is, the other one that looks about a third of a BMI unit worse.

7.5 Task 2 — Ten folds, one estimate, one standard error
Fifty repeats of an 80/20 split is not the usual way to do this, because the fifty test sets overlap heavily and each one wastes a fifth of the data at every repeat. Cross-validation partitions the rows instead: cut the training rows into ten parts, fit on nine, score on the one left out, ten times, so that every training row is scored exactly once and every score comes from a model that did not see it.
Note which rows are being cut. The test set is not in this at all — it stays closed.

RPython



# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(42)
folds <- vfold_cv(______, v = 10)        # which rows go into the folds?
folds

cv_res <- fit_resamples(wf, resamples = ______, metrics = metric_set(mae))
collect_metrics(cv_res)

cv_mean <- collect_metrics(cv_res)$mean
cv_se   <- collect_metrics(cv_res)$std_err
per_fold <- collect_metrics(cv_res, summarize = FALSE)$.estimate
c(folds_lowest = min(per_fold), folds_highest = max(per_fold))
c(model = cv_mean, baseline = mae_baseline,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * cv_mean / mae_baseline)







TipStuck?





vfold_cv() takes a data frame; the whole argument of this task is which frame it must not be given. fit_resamples() takes the same workflow you already built and the resamples object, and refits the recipe inside every fold. collect_metrics(..., summarize = FALSE) returns one row per fold rather than the average.






# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
folds = KFold(n_splits=______, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

fold_mae = -cross_val_score(build_pipeline(), ______[preds], ______["mass"],
                            cv=folds, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
cv_mean = fold_mae.mean()
cv_se   = fold_mae.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(10)
print(np.round(fold_mae, 3))
print(f"mean {cv_mean:.3f}, standard error {cv_se:.3f}, "
      f"folds {fold_mae.min():.3f} to {fold_mae.max():.3f}")
print(cv_mean, mae_baseline, 100 * cv_mean / mae_baseline)







TipStuck?





cross_val_score clones the estimator and refits it inside every fold, which is why it is handed build_pipeline() and not the pipe already fitted above. Scikit-learn’s scorers are oriented so that higher is better, hence the minus sign in front of a mean absolute error. The two blanks after it are the same frame, and it is not dia.






The ten-fold mean is 4.56 in R and 4.47 in Python, with a standard error of 0.15 and 0.17. Two things in that output are worth more than the mean.
First, the individual folds are more variable than the fifty splits were: 3.91 to 5.35 in R, 3.72 to 5.36 in Python. That is not a contradiction. Each fold scores about 60 rows where each split scored 151, so a single fold is a noisier measurement than a single split; what cross-validation gives you is not a quieter measurement but ten of them, averaged.
Second, count the fits. Fifty repeated splits cost fifty fits and returned a mean whose standard error is 0.03 to 0.04. Ten folds cost ten fits and returned a mean whose standard error is 0.15 to 0.17 — against a standard deviation of 0.21 to 0.28 for the single number you would otherwise have reported. Ten fits therefore bought a reduction in uncertainty of between a fifth and a half, not the factor of three that dividing by \(\sqrt{10}\) might have suggested, because the ten training sets overlap in nine tenths of their rows and the ten scores are not independent. On 604 rows and a linear model all of this is a second or two; on a model that takes an hour to fit, the choice between 10 folds, 5 folds and one split is a budget decision, and it is the usual reason published models are evaluated on one split.

text:
7.6 The result that should bother you
Everything above refits the preprocessing inside every fold, because the workflow and the Pipeline leave no other option. The common failure in practice is to do one preprocessing step by hand first — on the whole training set, once, because it is tidier — and then cross-validate what comes out. This is Chapter 6’s mistake moved inside the resampling loop, and the loop hides it.
Here is that mistake with a step that can carry real information: choosing which predictors to keep. Two hundred columns of pure random numbers are added to the training rows, the ten most correlated with BMI are selected, and the selected set is cross-validated. Then the same thing, with the selection repeated inside each fold.

RPython



set.seed(7)
noise <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(nrow(train) * 200), nrow(train), 200))
names(noise) <- paste0("noise", 1:200)
train_noise <- bind_cols(train["mass"], noise)
noise_cols  <- names(noise)

top_k <- function(d, k = 10) {
  r <- vapply(noise_cols, function(v) abs(cor(d[[v]], d$mass)), numeric(1))
  names(sort(r, decreasing = TRUE))[1:k]
}
chosen_once <- top_k(train_noise)        # chosen ONCE, on all the training rows

set.seed(99)
noise_folds <- vfold_cv(train_noise, v = 10)
fold_score <- function(sp, choose) {
  fit_rows <- analysis(sp); score_rows <- assessment(sp)
  m <- lm(reformulate(choose(fit_rows), "mass"), data = fit_rows)
  mean(abs(score_rows$mass - predict(m, score_rows)))
}

cv_outside <- mean(vapply(noise_folds$splits,
                          function(sp) fold_score(sp, function(d) chosen_once), numeric(1)))
cv_inside  <- mean(vapply(noise_folds$splits,
                          function(sp) fold_score(sp, top_k), numeric(1)))
cv_nothing <- mean(vapply(noise_folds$splits, function(sp)
  mean(abs(assessment(sp)$mass - mean(analysis(sp)$mass))), numeric(1)))

c(selected_outside = cv_outside, selected_inside = cv_inside,
  predict_the_mean = cv_nothing)

#> selected_outside  selected_inside predict_the_mean 
#>         5.390850         5.726338         5.469583



c(model = cv_outside, baseline = cv_nothing,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * cv_outside / cv_nothing)

#>               model            baseline percent_of_baseline 
#>            5.390850            5.469583           98.560545

c(model = cv_inside, baseline = cv_nothing,
  percent_of_baseline = 100 * cv_inside / cv_nothing)

#>               model            baseline percent_of_baseline 
#>            5.726338            5.469583          104.694247





from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_regression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(len(train), 200)),
                     columns=[f"noise{i}" for i in range(1, 201)],
                     index=train.index)
y = train["mass"]
noise_folds = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=99)

chosen_once = SelectKBest(f_regression, k=10).fit(noise, y)   # ONCE, on all of it
cv_outside = -cross_val_score(LinearRegression(),
                              noise.loc[:, chosen_once.get_support()], y,
                              cv=noise_folds,
                              scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()

cv_inside = -cross_val_score(Pipeline([("select", SelectKBest(f_regression, k=10)),
                                       ("model", LinearRegression())]),
                             noise, y, cv=noise_folds,
                             scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()

cv_nothing = -cross_val_score(DummyRegressor(strategy="mean"), noise, y,
                              cv=noise_folds,
                              scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()

print(cv_outside, cv_inside, cv_nothing)

#> 5.2592715996136805 5.748932066996416 5.371907196561035



print(cv_outside, cv_nothing, 100 * cv_outside / cv_nothing)

#> 5.2592715996136805 5.371907196561035 97.90324752781542

print(cv_inside, cv_nothing, 100 * cv_inside / cv_nothing)

#> 5.748932066996416 5.371907196561035 107.01845465008671





There is no signal in those 200 columns. They are random numbers, and no estimate of a model built from them should beat predicting the mean. Selected outside the loop, the cross-validated MAE is 5.39 in R and 5.26 in Python against a do-nothing 5.47 and 5.37: it beats the baseline, and the comparison says so. Selected inside the loop, the same ten folds, the same rule, the same random numbers, give 5.73 and 5.75 — worse than the baseline, which is the truth.

The selection step read the outcome. It was allowed to read it on all 604 training rows, including the 60 that each fold then held out for scoring.
So every fold’s held-out rows had already voted on which ten columns the model would use. The ten fits inside the loop are honest; the thing being evaluated is not a procedure applied to 544 rows, it is a procedure that already saw 604.
Cross-validation cannot detect this, because it only controls what happens after it is handed the data. A fitted step performed before the loop is invisible to it — the loop faithfully cross-validates a model that has already been given the answers.

The same mistake made with the imputation and scaling of Chapter 6 costs almost nothing, as Stretch 1 asks you to confirm. The difference is not how careless the analyst was. It is the same distinction Chapter 6 drew: a mean carries almost no row-specific information, and a choice made among 200 candidates by looking at the outcome carries a great deal.
Note also what the comparison showed: a pipeline built on nothing but random numbers still came out ahead of the baseline. Comparing against a baseline tells you whether a number is good; it cannot tell you whether the number was earned honestly. Nothing you print at the end can see what you did to the data before you printed it.

7.7 Task 3 — Three kinds of row
Assemble the three estimates of the same pipeline into one table, then write the sentence it supports. Keep the model_fits column: the three numbers are not equally cheap, and the table is useless without that.

RPython

tibble(
  estimate = c("one split (Exercise 2.4)", "50 repeated splits",
               "10-fold on the training rows"),
  value = c(mae_once, mean(maes), ______),
  uncertainty = c(NA, sd(maes), cv_se),
  model_fits = c(1, ______, 10)
)




# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
pd.DataFrame({
    "estimate": ["one split (Exercise 2.4)", "50 repeated splits",
                 "10-fold on the training rows"],
    "value": [mae_once, maes.mean(), ______],
    "uncertainty": [np.nan, maes.std(ddof=1), cv_se],
    "model_fits": [1, ______, 10],
}).round(3)




Then answer in writing, in one sentence each: which rows were fitted, which rows chose something, and which rows were spent in each of the three lines of your table. The middle role is empty in all three, because nothing has been chosen yet
That distinction is what the rest of the booklet runs on, and it is worth writing out once:








Role
Which rows
How often they can be used




Fitted
the analysis part of a fold, or the training set for the final model
as often as you like


Chose a setting
the assessment part of each fold
as often as you like, but a score computed on them is no longer held out


Spent
the test set
once, at the very end, and never again



A row may do the first two jobs in different folds; that is what resampling is. A row that does the third must never have done either of the others. Measure your own three estimates against that. The worked example opened the test set once. Task 1 opened fifty different test sets, which is defensible only because its purpose was to measure the spread and not to report a performance — the mean of those fifty is not a held-out number, because every row was fitted in some repeats and scored in others. Task 2 is the only one of the three that left the test rows closed.
